title: What is `explode()` vs `explode_outer()` — `explode` drops rows where the array is null/empty, `explode_outer` keeps them with nulls — and why should you filter and select BEFORE exploding (every row and column before the explode gets multiplied)?

s1_definition.profdef: `explode` and `explode_outer` both flatten an array (or map) column into multiple rows, producing one output row per element. The difference is null handling: `explode` drops a row entirely if its array is null or empty, so those parent rows disappear, whereas `explode_outer` keeps such rows, emitting a single row with a null in the exploded column. You should select only needed columns and filter before exploding because every surviving parent row and every carried column is duplicated once per array element, so exploding early multiplies data you did not need.
s1_definition.analogy: Each National Bank customer has a list of recent transactions. Exploding turns one customer row into one row per transaction. With `explode`, a customer who made no transactions (empty list) vanishes from the result, which can silently drop customers from a report. With `explode_outer`, that customer still appears once with a null transaction, so you keep everyone. And because exploding copies the customer's other columns onto every transaction row, you trim to only the columns you need first, or you waste memory copying everything.
s1_definition.oneliner: explode drops rows with null or empty arrays, explode_outer keeps them with nulls, and you filter and select before exploding because every parent row and column gets multiplied.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `explode` and `explode_outer` both flatten an array (or map) column into multiple rows, producing one output row per element. The difference is null handling: `explode` drops a row entirely if its array is null or empty, so those parent rows disappear, whereas `explode_outer` keeps such rows, emitting a single row with a null in the exploded column. You should select only needed columns and filter before exploding because every surviving parent row and every carried column is duplicated once per array element, so exploding early multiplies data you did not need.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Each National Bank customer has a list of recent transactions. Exploding turns one customer row into one row per transaction. With `explode`, a customer who made no transactions (empty list) vanishes from the result, which can silently drop customers from a report. With `explode_outer`, that customer still appears once with a null transaction, so you keep everyone. And because exploding copies the customer's other columns onto every transaction row, you trim to only the columns you need first, or you waste memory copying everything.

**One line to remember:** explode drops rows with null or empty arrays, explode_outer keeps them with nulls, and you filter and select before exploding because every parent row and column gets multiplied.

sections.s2_technical:
`F.explode(col)` takes an array column and produces one row per element, copying the other columns of the parent row onto each new row. If the array is null or empty, the parent row contributes zero rows to the output, so it is dropped. This behaves like an inner join between the row and its array elements.

`F.explode_outer(col)` is the left-outer equivalent: for a null or empty array it still emits one row for that parent with null in the exploded column, so no parent row is lost. The same pair exists for maps, where exploding yields key and value columns. There is also `posexplode` and `posexplode_outer`, which additionally emit the element's position index.

The choice matters for correctness. If a report must count every customer, using `explode` silently removes customers with no transactions, understating totals, so `explode_outer` is the safe default when parent rows must be preserved. If you only care about actual elements, `explode` is correct and smaller.

The performance guidance is about row and column multiplication. Explode is a one-to-many operation: a parent row with ten elements becomes ten rows, and every column you carried through is copied ten times. If you explode first and then select or filter, Spark materializes a wide, multiplied intermediate before discarding columns and rows. If instead you select only the columns you need and filter out rows you will discard before exploding, the multiplication applies to a much smaller, narrower dataset. For example `df.select("account_id", "recent_txns").filter(F.size("recent_txns") > 0).withColumn("amt", F.explode("recent_txns"))` keeps the intermediate tight.

A senior nuance: when the parent has several arrays, exploding each separately can create a cross-product explosion, so you either `arrays_zip` them first or explode one and handle the others with higher-order functions to avoid an accidental blow-up.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank's monthly statement report flattens each customer's transaction array into individual lines. A new customer with no transactions this month was silently dropped from the report because the team used `explode`. The auditors flagged the missing customer. This is exactly the explode-versus-explode_outer correctness issue.

Problem 2 — The customer records carry many wide columns (address, KYC fields). Exploding before trimming copied all of them onto every transaction line, wasting memory. This is exactly why we select before exploding.

Problem 3 — The report must include customers with zero transactions showing a null line. This is exactly what explode_outer provides.

What the code will do: a PySpark demo (`ExplodeDemo`) that builds customers for Rajesh (SAV2001) with transactions, Priya (CUR3001) with an empty list, and shows explode dropping Priya versus explode_outer keeping her, plus the select-before-explode pattern.

sections.s4d_java:
```python
# File: src/explode_demo.py
# Shows explode vs explode_outer and trim-before-explode for the National Bank.
import logging
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F
from pyspark.sql.types import (StructType, StructField, StringType,
                               ArrayType, DoubleType)
from flatten.statement_flattener import StatementFlattener

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("ExplodeDemo")

def spark_session() -> SparkSession:
    return SparkSession.builder.appName("ExplodeDemo").getOrCreate()

def main() -> None:
    spark = spark_session()
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("account_id", StringType()),
        StructField("kyc", StringType()),                 # wide column we will trim
        StructField("recent_txns", ArrayType(DoubleType()))])
    rows = [
        ("SAV2001", "KYC-FULL-DOC-BLOB-1", [50000.0, 12000.0]),
        ("CUR3001", "KYC-FULL-DOC-BLOB-2", []),            # empty list!
    ]
    df = spark.createDataFrame(rows, schema)
    flat = StatementFlattener(df)

    log.info("INNER explode (Priya with empty list is DROPPED):")
    flat.inner_explode().show()

    log.info("OUTER explode (Priya kept with null txn line):")
    flat.outer_explode().show()
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# File: src/flatten/statement_flattener.py
from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, functions as F

class StatementFlattener:
    """Flattens transaction arrays into statement lines."""
    def __init__(self, df: DataFrame):
        self.df = df

    def inner_explode(self) -> DataFrame:
        # SELECT only needed columns BEFORE exploding (drop wide 'kyc')
        trimmed = self.df.select("account_id", "recent_txns")
        return trimmed.withColumn("txn_amount", F.explode("recent_txns")) \
                      .drop("recent_txns")

    def outer_explode(self) -> DataFrame:
        trimmed = self.df.select("account_id", "recent_txns")
        return trimmed.withColumn("txn_amount", F.explode_outer("recent_txns")) \
                      .drop("recent_txns")
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: SAV2001 with two transactions and a wide KYC blob, CUR3001 with an empty transaction list.

Step 1: Both flatteners first select only `account_id` and `recent_txns`, dropping the wide `kyc` column so it is not copied onto every exploded line.

Step 2: `inner_explode` uses `explode`. SAV2001's two-element array becomes two rows (50000 and 12000). CUR3001's empty array contributes zero rows, so Priya disappears from the output entirely.

Step 3: `outer_explode` uses `explode_outer`. SAV2001 still becomes two rows. CUR3001's empty array now produces one row with a null `txn_amount`, so Priya is preserved.

Step 4: Because the trim happened first, the exploded intermediate carried only two columns, not the wide KYC blob, keeping memory small.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Both explode and explode_outer flatten an array or map column into multiple rows, emitting one output row per element and copying the parent row's other columns onto each new row. The difference is purely how they treat a null or empty array. Explode behaves like an inner join between the row and its elements, so a parent whose array is null or empty contributes zero rows and disappears from the result. Explode_outer behaves like a left-outer join, so that same parent still produces one row with a null in the exploded column and is never lost. There are posexplode variants too, which also give you the element's position index.

The choice is a correctness decision, not just a style preference. If a report must account for every customer, using explode silently drops customers who happened to have no transactions, which understates totals and gets flagged in an audit. So when parent rows must be preserved, explode_outer is the safe default, and I reserve plain explode for when I only care about actual elements and dropping empties is intended.

The performance guidance I always apply is to select and filter before exploding, because explode is a one-to-many operation. A parent row with ten elements becomes ten rows, and every column I carry through is copied ten times. If I explode first and trim later, Spark builds a wide, multiplied intermediate and then throws most of it away. At the National Bank of India our statement job once used explode and silently dropped a new customer with zero transactions, which the auditors caught, so we switched to explode_outer and also moved the column selection ahead of the explode so the heavy KYC fields were never copied onto every transaction line. The sentence I memorize is: explode drops null and empty arrays, explode_outer keeps them as nulls, and always trim and filter before you explode.
